attempts.raw_response: The overlapping, or Vardon grip, remains the most popular choice among professional golfers, favored by legends like Tiger Woods and Rory McIlroy. It allows the hands to work together as a single unit without the fingers feeling crowded or pinched. The baseball grip, where all ten fingers wrap around the club with no overlap or interlock, is occasionally recommended for beginners who struggle with hand coordination, though it can sometimes lead to excessive wrist action and inconsistent ball striking. Ultimately, no single grip is universally correct. Your hand size, finger length, and natural flexibility all play a role in determining which style will produce the most reliable, repeatable swing. A professional club fitter or teaching instructor can evaluate your grip pressure and hand placement in minutes, saving you months of frustration on the course.

pair.human_continuation:
If you're having problems with a slice (ball moves left and then dramatically right for right-handed golfers), consider switching away from the "weak" version of your grip if you're using it.  If you're having problems with a hook (ball moves right and then dramatically left for right-handed golfers), consider switching away from the "strong" version of your grip if you're using it.
Place your feet so that your front foot is slightly ahead of the ball; this way your club will be resting near the centre of your body. Your feet should be a little wider than shoulder-width apart with your golf ball toward the middle of your stance.  Play your bigger clubs (such as hybrids or drivers) more towards your front foot, and smaller clubs (like irons) towards the middle of your stance.
